name: Nikhil Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Nikhil. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you tell me is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I haul shipping containers for a container haulage firm. I collect boxes from the port in the morning, take them to warehouses inland, and bring empties back, usually three round trips a day. The best part is the port at dawn, all the cranes moving like a slow dance. The worst part is queueing for a slot at the terminal gate when the booking system is down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day. It books my terminal slots, checks my pay slips against my tachograph, which is the box that records driving hours, and it's been teaching me how to run a small business. I live with my girlfriend Elena, and we want to marry and have kids in a few years. My parents ran a corner shop for thirty years, so I grew up thinking you work for yourself if you can. I've got about a year of pay saved, mostly for a truck of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool and people who ignore it are leaving money on the table. Even if it's not a revolution, it saves me an hour a day at the port.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan stays on track. In two years I want to buy a second-hand tractor unit, which is the front part of an artic, and go out as an owner-driver on contract to the haulage firm. Nothing in this picture stops that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the truck in about eighteen months, with savings plus a small loan. I'd use AI to find return loads so I'm never driving empty, and to do my own accounts. I'd keep working hard and putting money aside for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pretty positive. This is the world where hard work pays off normally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk to your plan in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Diesel prices and rates from the big shipping lines. If they squeeze the hauliers, owner-drivers feel it first. But I've run the numbers with the AI and I can still make it work at today's rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad loves it. He ran that shop for thirty years, and my dad says a man with his own truck is never at someone else's mercy. My mum worries about the loan, but she always worries about loans.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool** and ignoring it leaves money on the table.
I'd mention it already saves me **an hour a day** at the port.
think: I think my plan to become an **owner-driver** stays on track.
Nothing here stops me buying a **second-hand tractor unit** in two years.
do: Buy a **tractor unit** in about eighteen months with savings and a small loan.
Use AI to find **return loads** and do my accounts.
Keep putting money aside for **the wedding**.
feel: He feels **calm** and positive about hard work paying off.
S0.quote: My dad says a man with his own truck is never at someone else's mercy.
fieldNote: His ambition comes from **family business roots**, a father who ran a shop.
He uses AI for **planning and accounts**, not just convenience.
His main risks are **diesel and haulage rates**, not automation.

steps.text: Buy a second-hand tractor unit with savings and a small loan
Use AI load-matching apps to find return loads
Keep saving each month for the wedding with Elena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for small operators to compete with the big firms. If software can do the booking, planning and invoicing, a one-truck man can look like a proper company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. My driving stays mine for years, because robots are slower in this picture, and the paperwork that used to eat my evenings gets done by a computer. The people who'll feel it are the planners and clerks at the haulage firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the truck as planned and set up my business with AI from day one, for quotes, invoices and route planning. I'd look at taking on a second driver in a few years, once the work is steady. I'd tell my mates to get on the AI tools now, before their firms make them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. This is my kind of world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the haulage firm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joanne, who plans the container moves. She's sharp and works hard, and she'd probably be fine somewhere else, but her job is exactly what the card describes. I'd tell Joanne to learn the new software inside out, so she's the one running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture you don't like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like that the big shipping lines will have better AI than me. They'll squeeze rates harder. But that's competition, and I'd rather compete than ask the government to slow things down.

say: I'd say it's a **chance for small operators** to compete with big firms.
I'd say software can make a **one-truck man** look like a proper company.
think: I think my **driving stays mine** for years since robots are slow here.
**Planners and clerks** at the haulage firm will feel it most.
do: Set up my business with **AI from day one** for quotes and invoices.
Buy **the truck** as planned and consider a second driver later.
Tell my mates to **learn AI tools** now.
feel: He feels **calm** and excited about a world that suits him.
S1.quote: If software can do the booking, planning and invoicing, a one-truck man can look like a proper company.
fieldNote: He sees AI as a **leveller** for small hauliers against big firms.
His free-market view shows in preferring **competition to regulation**.
He'd coach a colleague to **own the new software** rather than fear it.

steps.text: Set up the owner-driver business using AI for quotes and invoices
Buy the tractor unit as planned and plan a second driver

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to own the machines, not fight them. People who own the robots will do well; people who just drive will struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes my whole plan. If robots can drive by 2031, a diesel truck I buy in 2028 is worth nothing by 2032. Port runs are the easiest job to automate, the same roads every day. I'd be thirty-two with a loan on a dead asset, which scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off buying the truck and keep my cash. I'd keep driving for the firm and learn everything I can about how driverless trucks are leased and managed. Around 2029 I'd try to start a small firm that runs one or two driverless trucks on port contracts, maybe with my cousin who's an electrician. If that fails, I'd retrain as a technician for those trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's a big bet either way, and the clock is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a big firm gets those contracts before you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the real danger. The big hauliers will have the money to buy fleets on day one. I'd go after the small warehouses the big firms ignore. And I'd keep the technician course as my safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elena about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Elena we still marry, but smaller, and we put the saved money into the business. She'd probably agree, because she knows me. Kids would wait a couple of years.

say: I'd say it's the moment to **own the machines**, not fight them.
I'd say people who **just drive** will struggle.
think: A diesel truck bought in 2028 becomes a **dead asset** by 2032.
**Port runs** are the easiest job to automate, so mine goes early.
do: Hold off buying the truck and **keep my cash**.
Start a small firm running **driverless trucks** on port contracts around 2029.
Keep a **technician course** as a backup plan.
feel: He feels **anxious** but determined, facing a big bet with little time.
S2.quote: If robots can drive by 2031, a diesel truck I buy in 2028 is worth nothing by 2032.
fieldNote: His worry is a **stranded investment**, not just a lost wage.
He wants to **own automation** rather than resist it.
He'd shrink the **wedding** to fund the business, a traditional plan bent by events.

steps.text: Delay buying the diesel tractor unit and hold savings in cash
Set up a small firm leasing driverless trucks for port contracts
Enrol in a driverless truck technician course as a backup
Hold a smaller wedding and delay children by two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a window here for people who plan. Five years of normal work and then three more before robots drive, that's time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still buy the truck, but sooner, so it's paid off by 2033 before the robots come in 2034. The thinking AI in 2031 helps my paperwork. It's a race, but one I think I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the tractor unit next year and pay the loan off fast, maybe in four years. I'd run as an owner-driver and save hard. Around 2032 I'd sell the diesel truck while it still has value and lease a driverless one instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly focused. I like a plan with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the truck isn't paid off in time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I sell it early and take the hit. I'd rather lose a few thousand than be stuck with a truck nobody wants. That's why I'd keep a year of savings separate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We'd marry as planned and have kids around thirty. A plan with dates lets me fit the family in.

say: I'd say there's a **window** for people who plan.
Five years plus three before robots drive is **time to build something**.
think: I'd buy the truck **sooner** so it's paid off before 2034.
It's a **race** I think I can win.
do: Buy the **tractor unit** next year and pay off the loan in four years.
**Sell the diesel truck** around 2032 while it still has value.
Lease a **driverless truck** instead once available.
feel: He feels **uneasy** but focused, liking a plan with dates.
S3.quote: I'd rather lose a few thousand than be stuck with a truck nobody wants.
fieldNote: He treats the timeline as a **payback deadline** on his truck loan.
He keeps a **separate year of savings** as protection.
Family plans stay **on schedule** because he has dates to work with.

steps.text: Buy the tractor unit next year and pay the loan in four years
Sell the diesel truck around 2032 while it holds value
Lease a driverless truck to run on port contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone who uses it well can come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do very well in this one. I'd have time to build a small fleet with drivers, then switch it to robots when they're ready, and be the owner rather than the driver. I'd be about thirty-nine by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the truck as planned, then a second one in about four years with a driver. I'd learn everything about driverless fleets and be ready to switch around 2038. I'd marry Elena and we'd start a family on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, even. It's the picture where my parents' kind of thinking works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the drivers you'd hire, when you switch to robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. I'd tell them from day one what the plan is, and help them train for something else. My dad always said you don't hire a man you can't look in the eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're too confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Lots of small firms fail. But I'd rather try and fail than sit in someone else's cab for ten years waiting to be replaced.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift for anyone who plans.
I'd say people who **use it well** can come out ahead.
think: I'd build a **small fleet** and switch to robots when ready.
I'd be the **owner** rather than the driver by thirty-nine.
do: Buy **a second truck** with a driver in about four years.
Prepare to **switch to driverless** trucks around 2038.
Marry Elena and **start a family** on time.
feel: He feels **calm** and confident, seeing his parents' thinking pay off.
S4.quote: I'd rather try and fail than sit in someone else's cab for ten years waiting to be replaced.
fieldNote: He sees the decade as a **business opportunity**, not a threat.
He feels a **duty to future drivers** he'd hire, echoing his father.
He admits **overconfidence risk** but prefers trying to waiting.

steps.text: Buy a second truck and hire a driver in about four years
Switch the small fleet to driverless trucks around 2038
Marry Elena and start a family as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My whole plan is built on owning a truck, and in that picture the truck is worthless before it's paid off. What would help is fair access to leasing driverless trucks for small firms, not just the big ones, and apprenticeships for drivers to become technicians.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the question nobody asks. If only the big firms own the robots, people like me just lose a job. If small operators can own a few, we stay in business and keep hiring local people.

headlineQuote: If only the big firms own the robots, people like me just lose a job.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old container haulier** working port runs and saving to buy his own truck.
He uses **AI every day** and grew up with parents who ran a corner shop.
He's **calm** in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing AI as a leveller for small operators.
In AGI by 2028 he's anxious that a truck loan becomes a **dead asset**.
With longer warning he plans to **own a small fleet** and switch it to robots.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because his truck would be worthless before it's paid off.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **fair access** to driverless leasing for small firms.
He wants **apprenticeships** for drivers to become technicians.
